kurals.tamil:
கொலைமேற்கொண் டாரிற் கொடிதே அலைமேற்கொண்டு
அல்லவை செய்தொழுகும் வேந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Kolaimerkon daarir kodithe alaimerkondu
Allavai seythozhukum vendhu.
kurals.meaning: A king who makes a practice of harassing his people and keeps doing what is unjust is crueler than someone whose trade is murder.
kurals.elementary: Picture a playground bully who knocks you over once, and then picture a class monitor who is supposed to look after everyone but pushes kids around every single day. The monitor is worse, because the hurt never stops and the one person meant to protect you is the one hurting you. Valluvar says a cruel king is like that monitor, only much bigger.
kurals.university: The chapter is the mirror image of the preceding one, செங்கோன்மை (the straight sceptre, ch. 55): கொடுங்கோல் is the ‘bent’ rod of a ruler who governs by oppression. The key word அலை means harassing or tormenting, and Parimelazhagar glosses அலைமேற்கொண்டு as taking up, out of covetousness for wealth (பொருள்வெஃகி), the business of harassing the subjects. His reason for the comparison is that the murderer’s harm lasts a moment, whereas the tyrant’s is lifelong, so ‘harassment is crueller than killing’. He also notes the grammatical point that வேந்து, a neuter-class noun, is used here of a person (திணை/பால் மயக்கம்). Manakkudavar gives substantially the same reading, while Solomon Pappaiah stresses greed for the people’s property. The text is uniform across ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and thirukkural.com; the older continuous text on thirukkural-thamizh.org shows the unsplit sandhi forms யலைமேற்கொண் / டல்லவை.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kamsa, king of Mathura, imprisoned his own father, persecuted the Yadus and had the infant children of his sister Devaki put to death one after another, until Krishna, the child he feared, grew up and killed him.
hinduism.explanation: In the Bhagavata Purana, Kamsa is the classic tyrant whose power is used against the very people and kin he should protect.
hinduism.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s cruel king, Kamsa does more harm than an ordinary killer because the whole kingdom lives under his fear.
hinduism._accuracy_note: A strong narrative example of a king worse than a murderer; the text does not make the Kural’s explicit comparison.

christianity.quote_or_event: “As a roaring lion, and a ranging bear; so is a wicked ruler over the poor people.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb compares a wicked ruler to beasts of prey loose among the helpless.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks an unjust ruler alongside the most dangerous killers.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close in spirit; the proverb makes a comparison rather than the Kural’s ‘worse than’ ranking.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing a sector among them, slaughtering their [newborn] sons and keeping their females alive. Indeed, he was of the corrupters.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an’s portrait of Pharaoh is its central image of a ruler who turns state power into ongoing oppression of his own subjects.
islam.tie_back: Pharaoh is the Kural’s tyrant exactly: a king whose rule is itself a form of killing.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close thematic match; verified verbatim against the Saheeh International text.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ezekiel says that the princes of Jerusalem have become like wolves tearing their prey, shedding blood and destroying lives for the sake of dishonest gain.
judaism.explanation: The prophet accuses the rulers themselves, not outside enemies, of preying on the people for profit.
judaism.tie_back: It matches Parimelazhagar’s reading that the tyrant harasses his subjects out of greed for their wealth.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; strong match on rulers as predators driven by gain.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The whole nation sleeps badly, when the king is unprincipled.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that when the king goes astray, his officials and then the whole people follow, just as a herd follows its lead bull.
buddhism.tie_back: The whole nation suffering day and night echoes Parimelazhagar’s point that the tyrant’s harm never stops, unlike a killer’s single act.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.70, Adhammika Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified wording; it describes the nationwide suffering, not the murderer comparison.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Lycaon of Arcadia, a cruel ruler, served human flesh to Zeus to test him; Zeus destroyed his house and turned him into a wolf whose savage nature matched his reign.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells the story as the first example of human wickedness that moves the gods to punish the world.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A king who becomes a literal wolf pictures the Kural’s claim that a tyrant is worse than an ordinary killer.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good image of the king as a predator; Lycaon’s crime is impiety as well as cruelty.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates describes how the people’s ‘protector’ becomes a tyrant: once he has tasted the blood of his own citizens through unjust trials and killings, he turns into a wolf, as in the Arcadian legend.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato the tyrant is the worst of men because he turns the power of the state against those he rules.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato and Valluvar agree that the ruler who preys on his own people is worse than a common criminal.

kurals.tamil:
வேலொடு நின்றான் இடுவென் றதுபோலும்
கோலொடு நின்றான் இரவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Velodu nindraan iduven rathupolum
Kolodu nindraan iravu.
kurals.meaning: When a ruler who holds the sceptre asks his subjects for money, it is like a robber standing with a spear on a lonely road and saying ‘Hand it over’.
kurals.elementary: If a big kid holding a stick says ‘Can I please have your lunch?’, it isn’t really a question, because you know what happens if you say no. Valluvar says that when a king with power over you ‘asks’ for extra money, it is the same as a robber demanding it.
kurals.university: The image is of the solitary highwayman (வேலொடு நின்றான்) and the king ‘standing with the rod’ (கோலொடு நின்றான்), the rod here meaning the power to punish (ஒறுத்தல் தொழில்). Parimelazhagar draws two inferences: ‘standing with a spear’ implies the robber is alone on a deserted road, and the word இரவு (begging, request) shows that what the king asks for is not the lawful revenue (இறைப்பொருள் அன்மை). Because the king’s request carries an unspoken threat to punish anyone who refuses, even ‘asking’ becomes tyranny; he adds that kurals 551-552 together state the fault of tyranny itself. Manakkudavar reads கோலொடு நிற்றல் as standing in the posture of one who administers justice, and adds that even a voluntary-seeming levy above the fixed dues is like robbery on the road. Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take the couplet as a comment on extortionate taxation. The text is the same across the sources consulted.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Manu warns that a king who gives no protection yet takes his share of the produce, his taxes, tolls and fines will soon sink into hell, since he takes on the sins of the people he fails to protect.
hinduism.explanation: In the Dharmashastra, taxation is fair only as payment for protection; without it, the levy becomes a sin.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point: a levy without righteous rule is just robbery.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong doctrinal parallel; paraphrased from Bühler.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he said unto them, Exact no more than that which is appointed you. … Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages.”
christianity.explanation: John the Baptist tells tax collectors and soldiers, the two faces of state power, not to extort beyond what is due.
christianity.tie_back: Like Valluvar, John treats demands backed by force above the lawful due as extortion.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on extortion by officials; verified KJV wording.

islam.quote_or_event: After the woman of Ghamid was stoned for adultery she had confessed, the Prophet said her repentance was so sincere that even a collector of unjust taxes (ṣāḥib maks) would be forgiven if he repented like that.
islam.explanation: The hadith treats the taker of unjust levies as the extreme case of a grave sinner.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s view that exacting money by the power of office is among the worst wrongs.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the condemnation of maks is implied through comparison, not stated as a direct teaching.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Israel asks for a king, Samuel warns that the king will take their sons, their daughters, their best fields and vineyards, and a tenth of their grain and flocks, and they will become his servants.
judaism.explanation: The prophet describes kingship as, by nature, taking from the people.
judaism.tie_back: Samuel’s ‘he will take’ corresponds to the king’s demand in the Kural, which his subjects cannot refuse.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; strong parallel on royal exaction.

buddhism.quote_or_event: A wise chaplain advises King Mahāvijita that a kingdom plagued by bandits cannot be cured by more levies and punishments; instead the king should give seed to farmers, capital to traders and wages to officials, and the country then becomes prosperous and safe.
buddhism.explanation: The Kūṭadanta Sutta sets out a Buddhist economics of rule that relies on giving, not taking.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the positive counterpart to the Kural’s warning against a king who rules by demanding.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Complementary rather than identical: it recommends the opposite policy instead of condemning extortion directly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On his road to Athens the young Theseus killed a series of highway robbers, including Sciron, who made travellers wash his feet and then kicked them off the cliff, and Sinis the pine-bender. By clearing the road he showed what kind of king he would be.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Plutarch’s account, a true ruler is the one who ends robbery on the roads, not the one who practises it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Valluvar’s image of the road robber stands for the king who has forgotten this duty.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The highway robber image is shared, but the myth praises the king who kills robbers rather than comparing a king to one.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Justice being taken away, then, what are kingdoms but great robberies? For what are robberies themselves, but little kingdoms?”
philosophy.explanation: Augustine argues that without justice, the state is simply a robber band on a larger scale.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s simile turned into a general principle: a king without justice is just a robber.
philosophy.source: Augustine, City of God IV.4 (trans. Marcus Dods)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; verified against the New Advent text.

kurals.tamil:
நாடொறும் நாடி முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்
நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Naadorum naadi muraiseyyaa mannavan
Naadorum naadu kedum.
kurals.meaning: A king who does not look into wrongs every day and give justice will see his country decline a little more every day.
kurals.elementary: If you never look after a garden, weeds creep in a little each day until the flowers are gone. A king who doesn’t check every day for unfair things happening, and fix them, lets his whole country slowly go to ruin in the same way.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on நாள் / நாடு: நாடொறும் (daily, from நாள் + தொறும்) and நாடி (examining, from நாடு-தல்), then நாடு (country). Parimelazhagar glosses: the king who does not daily examine the wrongs occurring in his land and render fitting justice will daily ‘lose’ his country. He explains that since the country is a limb (உறுப்பு) of the king, the verb ‘perish’ is attributed to him, and that ‘losing’ here means failing to enjoy its fruits (பயன் எய்தாமை). He records an alternative construal, ‘the king’s country perishes daily’ (மன்னவன் நாடு நாள்தொறும் கெடும்), which Manakkudavar and Kalaignar adopt. For the first word, thirukkural.com prints the unassimilated form நாள்தொறும், while ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give the sandhi form நாடொறும்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya divides the king’s day into eighths and assigns him times to hear the petitions of citizens and country people. He warns that a king who makes petitioners wait at his door, or who is hard to reach, causes confusion in the state and disaffection among the people.
hinduism.explanation: For the Arthashastra, attending daily to the people’s complaints is the core routine of kingship.
hinduism.tie_back: It sets out as a timetable the daily enquiry that Valluvar says keeps the kingdom from decaying.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-exact parallel on the king’s daily hearing of grievances; paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus tells of an unjust judge who for a long time ignored a widow pleading for justice, and gave way only because she kept coming back.
christianity.explanation: The parable assumes that a judge who neglects the cries of the weak is unjust.
christianity.tie_back: The judge is the negligent ruler of the Kural, who does not look into wrongs day by day.
christianity._accuracy_note: The parable is mainly about persistent prayer; the neglectful judge is only a secondary parallel.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that any ruler given charge of people who does not look after them with sincere care will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.
islam.explanation: The hadith makes neglect of one’s subjects a grave moral failure, not just bad administration.
islam.tie_back: It condemns the same inattentive ruler whom the Kural says will slowly lose his realm.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; close on the ruler’s duty of continual care, while the sanction is otherworldly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “O house of David, thus saith the LORD: Execute justice in the morning, And deliver the spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor, Lest My fury go forth like fire…”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah tells the royal house to do justice every morning and to rescue the robbed.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Justice in the morning’ is the Kural’s daily enquiry and justice, with ruin as the price of neglect.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close, down to the daily timing; verified on Sefaria.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Cakkavatti Sīhanāda Sutta a king fails to give wealth to the needy; poverty spreads, then theft, then weapons, killing and lying, and the lifespan and beauty of the people decline generation after generation.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta traces how one royal neglect grows step by step into a society’s collapse.
buddhism.tie_back: It is a long-scale version of the Kural’s ‘day by day the country perishes’.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel on gradual decline from royal neglect; paraphrased.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ play, Thebes is struck by blight and plague because the murder of King Laius was never investigated; Creon admits the Sphinx made the city set aside the unsolved crime.
greek_mythology.explanation: The city suffers because a wrong was never looked into and put right.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatizes the Kural’s warning that unexamined wrongs slowly destroy the land.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The idea of neglected justice is present, but the play’s focus is fate and pollution.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle calls the ruler the guardian of justice, and says that for this reason a true ruler does not take more than his share and labours for others.
philosophy.explanation: Rule, for Aristotle, is justified only by constant attention to what is just.
philosophy.tie_back: A ruler who fails at this guardianship is the one the Kural says wears his country away.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics V.6, 1134b (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Right principle, but it lacks the Kural’s emphasis on daily vigilance and gradual ruin.

kurals.tamil:
கூழுங் குடியும் ஒருங்கிழக்கும் கோல்கோடிச்
சூழாது செய்யும் அரசு.
kurals.transliteration:
Koozhung kudiyum orungizhakkum kolkodich
Choozhaathu seyyum arasu.
kurals.meaning: A king who bends justice and acts without thinking about the consequences loses both his wealth and his people at once.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a lemonade stand owner who cheats customers without thinking ahead. Soon the customers stop coming, and with them goes the money. Valluvar says a careless, unfair king loses his treasure and his people together, because the people are where the treasure comes from.
kurals.university: கூழ் (literally gruel or food) stands for wealth, and குடி for the subjects. Parimelazhagar makes the pairing precise: கூழ் is the wealth already amassed, and குடி is the people who are the source of wealth yet to be earned, so the tyrant loses past and future income together. சூழாது means ‘without deliberating’ on what will follow, and கோல்கோடி means ‘bending the sceptre’; he notes கோடி stands for the infinitive கோட. He adds that the next couplet gives the cause of losing wealth already amassed. Manakkudavar marks this couplet as stating the fault that comes from acting without deliberation. Kalaignar reads குடி more loosely as ‘the people’s esteem’. The text is the same across the sources consulted, and Pope’s rendering ‘who counsel doth refuse’ follows the sense of சூழாது.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That king who is illiberal, and without affection, who afflicts his subjects by undue chastisements, and who is rash in his acts, soon meets with destruction.”
hinduism.explanation: The sage Vamadeva warns King Vasumanas that harsh, rash rule leads straight to ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: Rash action (சூழாது) and unjust punishment (கோல்கோடி) are the two faults the Kural names.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Śānti Parva, Section XCII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close match; verified against the Ganguli text on sacred-texts.com.

christianity.quote_or_event: Thomas Aquinas argues that tyrannical rule cannot last long, because it is hateful to the multitude and rests on fear, which is a weak foundation, so tyrants are soon overthrown.
christianity.explanation: For Aquinas, oppression undermines the very base of the ruler’s power.
christianity.tie_back: It agrees with the Kural that the unjust king loses his people, and with them his hold on power.
christianity.source: Thomas Aquinas, De Regno (On Kingship) I.10
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; good fit on the loss of people’s loyalty, less on the loss of wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: Of Pharaoh and his people after they pursued the Israelites, the Qur’an says: “So We removed them from gardens and springs” and from treasures and an honoured station.
islam.explanation: Pharaoh’s oppression ends with the loss of all his wealth and power at a single stroke.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘loses both wealth and people at once’.
islam._accuracy_note: Verse 57 verified verbatim, verse 58 paraphrased; the loss is presented as divine punishment, not natural consequence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke; my father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.”
judaism.explanation: King Rehoboam rejects the elders’ advice to lighten the people’s burden, and the ten northern tribes break away from him.
judaism.tie_back: He is exactly the king who ‘does not deliberate’ and bends the rod, and so loses most of his people and revenue in one day.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one narrative illustration; verified on Sefaria.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells King Ajātasattu’s minister that the Vajjians will not decline as long as they meet often, act in harmony, keep their established laws, and honour and listen to their elders.
buddhism.explanation: The ‘conditions of non-decline’ tie a state’s survival to consultation and just custom.
buddhism.tie_back: They are the exact opposite of the Kural’s king, who acts without counsel and bends justice.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Positive counterpart rather than a direct statement of loss; paraphrased.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Creon, king of Thebes, ignores his son Haemon and the prophet Tiresias and persists in an unjust decree. By the end he has lost his son and his wife, and the city has turned against him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sophocles shows a ruler who refuses counsel and loses everything at once.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Creon’s fall is the Kural’s king who ‘acts without deliberation’ and loses all together.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on refusing counsel and sudden total loss; the losses are family rather than treasury.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that tyranny and oligarchy are the shortest-lived of all constitutions, and that most tyrannies have lasted only a short time.
philosophy.explanation: His survey of Greek history finds oppressive rule unstable by nature.
philosophy.tie_back: It gives historical support to the Kural’s claim that the bent sceptre brings quick and total loss.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; general rather than specific to wealth and people.

kurals.tamil:
அல்லற்பட்டு ஆற்றாது அழுதகண் ணீரன்றே
செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை.
kurals.transliteration:
Allarpattu aatraathu azhuthakan neerandre
Selvaththaith theykkum padai.
kurals.meaning: The tears of people who suffer and cannot bear it any longer are the weapon that wears away an oppressive king’s wealth.
kurals.elementary: Water dripping on a stone for a long, long time can wear a hole right through it. Valluvar says the tears of people treated unfairly are like that water: drop by drop, they wear away the riches of the ruler who made them cry.
kurals.university: அல்லல் is distress, ஆற்றாது ‘unable to bear it’, and படை ‘army’ or ‘weapon’. The verb தேய்க்கும் (wears away, grinds down) has led translators to render படை as a file or saw (Pope has ‘sharp instruments’, and the prose translation ‘a saw’). Parimelazhagar calls the figure ஏகதேச உருவகம் (partial metaphor): Valluvar does not say ‘the tree of wealth’, but the verb implies it. He explains that the destructive work really done by the sin of causing suffering is credited to the tears that are its sign, ‘because nothing is crueller than those tears’, and that the sense is that the wealth wastes away quickly. He groups kurals 553-556 as stating the evils that befall the tyrant himself. The text is the same across the sources consulted.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Take care that the eyes of the weak do not burn thee with thy kinsmen. In a race scorched by the eyes of the weak, no children take birth.”
hinduism.explanation: The sage Utathya warns King Mandhatri that the grief of the oppressed has a power that can destroy even the mightiest ruler.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural’s idea exactly: the suffering of the weak becomes a weapon against the tyrant.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Śānti Parva, Section XCI (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one parallel; the same passage also mentions tears. Verified on sacred-texts.com.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.”
christianity.explanation: James warns oppressive rich men that the cries of those they cheated have reached God, and that their riches are already rotting.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, the cry of the wronged is what destroys the oppressor’s wealth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close; the target is rich employers rather than kings. Verified KJV wording.

islam.quote_or_event: When sending Mu‘ādh to Yemen, the Prophet told him to beware of the supplication of the oppressed, for there is no barrier between it and God.
islam.explanation: The cry of the wronged goes straight to God and brings about justice.
islam.tie_back: Like the tears in the Kural, the prayer of the oppressed works as a weapon against the unjust.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child. If thou afflict them in any wise—for if they cry at all unto Me, I will surely hear their cry— My wrath shall wax hot, and I will kill you with the sword…”
judaism.explanation: The Torah promises that God hears the cry of the defenceless and turns it against their oppressor.
judaism.tie_back: The victim’s cry becomes the ‘sword’, just as in the Kural the tears become the army.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close; verified on Sefaria (KJV numbers these verses 22:22-24).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like fine dust thrown against the wind, evil falls back upon that fool who offends an inoffensive, pure and guiltless man.”
buddhism.explanation: Harm done to the innocent comes back on the one who does it.
buddhism.tie_back: In the Kural, the suffering a tyrant inflicts comes back to wear away his own wealth.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified wording; general moral recoil rather than the specific image of tears.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phoenix tells Achilles of the Prayers (Litai), lame and wrinkled daughters of Zeus, who follow after Ruin. If a man rejects them, they go to Zeus and ask that Ruin should dog that man until he pays in full.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Homer, the rejected pleas of suppliants become a force that brings ruin on the hard-hearted.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is close to the Kural’s idea that unanswered distress turns into a destructive power.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the pleas are a suppliant’s, not an oppressed people’s.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero argues that fear is a poor guardian of lasting power and goodwill a faithful one, and that no amount of power can withstand the hatred of the many, as the fall of tyrants shows.
philosophy.explanation: For Cicero, the resentment of the oppressed eventually overthrows even the strongest ruler.
philosophy.tie_back: It gives the Kural’s ‘tears as an army’ a political explanation.

kurals.tamil:
மன்னர்க்கு மன்னுதல் செங்கோன்மை அஃதின்றேல்
மன்னாவாம் மன்னர்க் கொளி.
kurals.transliteration:
Mannarkku mannuthal sengonmai akhthindrel
Mannaavaam mannark koli.
kurals.meaning: Just rule is what makes a king’s fame last; without it, his glory will not endure.
kurals.elementary: A trophy you won by cheating doesn’t feel like yours, and people stop cheering once they find out. Valluvar says a king’s glory is like that: only fair, honest rule keeps it shining, and without fairness it fades away.
kurals.university: The couplet repeats the root மன்- ‘to endure’ for effect: மன்னர் (kings), மன்னுதல் (enduring) and மன்னா (will not endure). ஒளி (light, lustre) means renown. Parimelazhagar supplies the instrumental case lost by elision: ‘kings’ fame endures by the straight sceptre’. He cites Nāṉmaṇikkaṭikai 17 (‘if you wish to endure in this world, plant fame’) to show that fame is what makes a person endure. He explains the plural (ஒளி taken as many forms of fame, from victory, generosity and so on) and concludes that if their fame does not last, the kings themselves do not last. Some continuous-text editions read the sandhi form அஃதின்றேன் and மன்னாவா மன்னர்க் for அஃதின்றேல் மன்னாவாம். Manakkudavar puts this couplet first in the ‘faults’ series, taking the loss of glory as the first penalty of misrule.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhishma tells how the first true king, Prithu, was called rājā because he gladdened (rañjana) all the people by protecting them, the earth yielding abundantly under his righteous rule.
hinduism.explanation: The very title ‘king’ is said to come from pleasing and protecting the people.
hinduism.tie_back: As the Kural says, a king’s standing and fame rest wholly on righteous rule.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Śānti Parva, Section LIX (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from memory of the Ganguli text; the etymology is traditional and the link to lasting fame is implied.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The king that faithfully judgeth the poor, his throne shall be established for ever.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb ties the permanence of a throne to just judgement of the powerless.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim: just rule is what makes a king endure.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; verified KJV wording.

islam.quote_or_event: “O David, indeed We have made you a successor upon the earth, so judge between the people in truth and do not follow [your own] desire, as it will lead you astray from the way of Allah.”
islam.explanation: David’s authority as ruler is given on the condition that he judges with truth.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes just judgement the condition of lasting rule.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified wording; it is about the condition of authority rather than fame.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are three crowns: the crown of Torah, the crown of priesthood, and the crown of royalty, but the crown of a good name supersedes them all.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Shimon ranks a good name above every office, kingship included.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise holds that royal glory is empty unless the good name that comes from just rule upholds it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified wording; strong on name above crown, less explicit on justice as its source.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Jātakas list ten royal virtues (dasa rāja-dhamma): generosity, moral conduct, self-sacrifice, honesty, gentleness, self-restraint, freedom from anger, non-violence, patience and non-opposition to the right. A king who keeps them is praised and his reign prospers.
buddhism.explanation: In Buddhist tradition, a king’s greatness is measured by these ten virtues.
buddhism.tie_back: They spell out the ‘straight sceptre’ that the Kural says alone makes a king’s fame last.
buddhism.source: Jātaka No. 534, Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka (ed. E. B. Cowell)
buddhism._accuracy_note: The list is traditional and attested in the Jātakas; the link to lasting fame is implied rather than stated.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Plato’s closing myth, Minos, Rhadamanthys and Aeacus, kings remembered for their justice in life, are appointed after death to judge the dead, while the souls of tyrants are the most scarred and incurable.
greek_mythology.explanation: Only just kings gain an honour that lasts forever; unjust rulers become eternal warnings.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s point that only just rule makes a king’s glory endure.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the glory is posthumous and mythic.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells Nero that a ruler’s one impregnable defence is the love of his citizens, and that clemency secures a lasting good name where cruelty leaves only a hated memory.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic argues that mercy and justice, not force, make a reign secure and its memory honoured.
philosophy.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s claim that only the straight sceptre makes a ruler’s glory last.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; close on security and reputation.

kurals.tamil:
துளியின்மை ஞாலத்திற்கு எற்றற்றே வேந்தன்
அளியின்மை வாழும் உயிர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Thuliyinmai gnaalaththirku etratre vendhan
Aliyinmai vaazhum uyirkku.
kurals.meaning: What drought is to the world, a king’s lack of kindness is to the people who live under him.
kurals.elementary: When it doesn’t rain for a long time, plants wilt, rivers shrink, and animals go thirsty. A king without kindness makes his people wilt in just the same way, because his care is like rain to them.
kurals.university: துளி (a drop) stands for rain by synecdoche. Parimelazhagar says the word was chosen because a drop is the most telling part of rain. அளி means gracious, tender care, and உயிர் (life, living beings) here stands for the subjects. The construction எற்று… அற்றே (‘of what kind…? just so’) makes a rhetorical comparison. Parimelazhagar notes that this couplet puts negatively what kural 542 had said positively: the whole world lives looking to the sky for rain, and the subjects look to the king’s sceptre. He groups kurals 557-558 as stating the evils that fall on those who live in the tyrant’s land. Solomon Pappaiah reads அளி more broadly as ‘righteous governance’. The text is the same across the sources consulted.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Manu tells the king to act like Indra: as Indra sends plentiful rain in the four months of the rainy season, so the king should shower benefits on his kingdom.
hinduism.explanation: The ‘vow of Indra’ makes the king’s generosity the political counterpart of rain.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the positive form of the Kural’s image: the king’s kindness is rain to his people.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-identical rain and king analogy; paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “…for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus points to God’s rain, given freely to everyone, as the model for goodness that does not pick and choose.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural calls a ruler’s kindness a kind of rain; here God’s rain is the pattern of such kindness.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified wording; the rain and kindness link is shared, but the subject is God, not kings.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that whoever is not merciful to people, God will not be merciful to him.
islam.explanation: Mercy toward others is made the condition of receiving God’s mercy.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s merciless king cuts himself off from mercy, and his people from relief.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a general teaching on mercy, not specifically about rulers or rain.

judaism.quote_or_event: “May he come down like rain upon the mown grass, as showers that water the earth.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm for the king prays that his just rule will refresh the land as rain does.
judaism.tie_back: It is the same image as the Kural: a king’s gracious rule is rain for his people.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one image; verified on Sefaria.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Lotus Sutra, the Buddha compares his teaching to a great rain cloud that pours down equally on every herb, shrub and tree, each drinking according to its kind.
buddhism.explanation: Compassion is pictured as rain that nourishes every living thing without discrimination.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘kindness as rain’ is the same image, applied to a king.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the image is shared, but the context is spiritual teaching, not government.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Demeter withdrew in grief and anger, she made the earth bear no crops, and mankind would have perished of famine if Zeus had not brought her daughter back.
greek_mythology.explanation: When the goddess who sustains life holds back her care, the whole world goes hungry.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s drought, the withdrawal of care from above leaves every living being in distress.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Parallel structure (withheld care leads to famine), but it is about a goddess, not a king.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Answering Thrasymachus, Socrates argues that a true ruler, like a true shepherd, looks to the good of those in his care, not his own profit.
philosophy.explanation: Rule is defined as care for the ruled.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s king without அளி (gracious care) fails the very definition of ruling.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the principle matches but it lacks the rain image.

kurals.tamil:
இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை முறைசெய்யா
மன்னவன் கோற்கீழ்ப் படின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Inmaiyin innaathu udaimai muraiseyyaa
Mannavan korkeezhp padin.
kurals.meaning: Under the sceptre of an unjust king, having wealth brings more misery than having nothing.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a class where a mean monitor takes the best toy from anyone who brings one. Soon, the kids who bring nice toys are the most worried ones. Valluvar says that under a greedy king, being rich becomes more dangerous than being poor.
kurals.university: The paradox turns on இன்மை (having nothing) and உடைமை (possessing). Parimelazhagar explains it by describing what the covetous king does: those who own property are the ones who suffer seizures, torture and binding ‘till the hands ache’ (கைந்நோவ யாப்புண்டல்), so under such a ruler wealth is worse than poverty. He applies it to everyone (யாவர்க்கும்), not just the rich, and groups kurals 557-558 as stating the evils that fall on those who live in the tyrant’s land. Manakkudavar agrees (‘even the wealthy suffer’) and counts 557-559 as the evils of failing to do justice. கோற்கீழ்ப் படின் means ‘if one falls under the sceptre’. The text is the same across the sources consulted.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhishma teaches that a king should draw revenue gently, as a bee gathers honey without harming the flower, or as one milks a cow without cutting the udder, so that the people can go on producing wealth.
hinduism.explanation: Greedy taxation that crushes the producers destroys the source of all wealth.
hinduism.tie_back: Under a king who ignores this, wealth becomes a burden, which is exactly the Kural’s point.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Śānti Parva, Section LXXXVIII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; it states the rule for good kings rather than the misery under bad ones.

christianity.quote_or_event: Naboth refused to sell King Ahab the vineyard he had inherited, so Queen Jezebel had false witnesses accuse him. He was stoned to death and the king took the vineyard.
christianity.explanation: Naboth’s small property was exactly what brought the unjust king’s power down on him.
christianity.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural’s paradox: under an unjust king, owning something is more dangerous than owning nothing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near-exact narrative illustration; this is a shared Hebrew Bible text, not a distinctively Christian one.

islam.quote_or_event: “As for the ship, it belonged to poor people working at sea. So I intended to cause defect in it as there was after them a king who seized every [good] ship by force.”
islam.explanation: Al-Khidr damages the poor men’s boat to save it, because a sound boat would be taken by the tyrant king.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s paradox exactly: under an unjust king, having something good is worse than having less.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And they covet fields, and seize them; And houses, and take them away; Thus they oppress a man and his house, Even a man and his heritage.”
judaism.explanation: Micah condemns the powerful who take land and houses from ordinary people.
judaism.tie_back: Under such rulers, a man’s property is exactly what draws oppression, as the Kural says.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified wording; the oppressors are the powerful generally, not only the king.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha describes a man who works hard to gain wealth and then suffers anxiety guarding it, thinking ‘How can I keep kings and thieves from taking it?’, and grieves bitterly when kings seize it.
buddhism.explanation: Among the dangers of wealth, the sutta names seizure by kings as a standard source of suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: It spells out why property can hurt more than poverty under a grasping ruler.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; close, though the sutta’s aim is to show the danger of sense-desire.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Asked for advice on ruling, the tyrant Thrasybulus led Periander’s messenger through a cornfield, silently cutting off every ear of grain that stood above the rest. Periander understood that he should do away with the most prominent citizens.
greek_mythology.explanation: Under tyranny, standing out through wealth or distinction makes a person a target.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is a vivid picture of the Kural’s paradox: under the cruel sceptre, the well-off suffer most.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Historical anecdote rather than myth; strong thematic match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that tyrants deliberately impoverish their subjects, through heavy taxes and great public works like the pyramids of Egypt, so that the people are too busy and poor to plot against them.
philosophy.explanation: He sees stripping people of property as a deliberate tool of tyranny.
philosophy.tie_back: It explains why, as the Kural says, wealth becomes a misery under such a king.

kurals.tamil:
முறைகோடி மன்னவன் செய்யின் உறைகோடி
ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Muraikodi mannavan seyyin uraikodi
Ollaathu vaanam peyal.
kurals.meaning: If a king rules against justice, the seasons go wrong and the sky will not send its rain.
kurals.elementary: Think of a team captain who cheats. Soon nobody plays well, the whole game falls apart, and it feels as if even luck has left. The old poets said that when a king is unfair, even the rain stops coming on time.
kurals.university: The couplet repeats கோடி (bending): the king ‘bends’ justice (முறைகோடி) and the rain ‘bends’ from its season (உறைகோடி). Parimelazhagar notes that both forms stand for the infinitive கோட, glosses உறைகோடுதல் as ‘failing to rain at the time for rain’, and says the cause is given in the next couplet. Classical commentators take this as a real cosmic link between royal righteousness and the monsoon, a belief widespread in Indian thought. Kalaignar instead reads உறை as reservoirs and rain-storage works that fall to ruin under misrule, so the rain cannot be stored and used. The text is the same across the sources consulted, apart from sandhi spacing in the older continuous text (செய்யி னுறைகோடி யொல்லாது).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If the deity of the clouds pours rain seasonably and the king acts virtuously, the prosperity that ensues maintain the subjects in felicity.” … “It is the king who constitutes the age.”
hinduism.explanation: The sage Utathya teaches that whether the age is Krita or Kali, a golden age or a dark one, depends on the king’s conduct, and that seasonable rain goes together with a virtuous king.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the same cosmic link the Kural draws between a crooked king and failing rain.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Śānti Parva, Section XCI (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close; verified on sacred-texts.com (two sentences from the same passage).

christianity.quote_or_event: “Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain: and it rained not on the earth by the space of three years and six months.”
christianity.explanation: James recalls the drought under King Ahab, whose idolatry and injustice Elijah opposed.
christianity.tie_back: In the biblical story, as in the Kural, an unrighteous king’s reign is marked by the heavens holding back their rain.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified wording; the drought comes through prophetic prayer against Ahab, not automatically from misrule.

islam.quote_or_event: A hadith lists sins that bring collective punishment: when people cheat in weights and measures, they are struck by famine, hardship and the oppression of the ruler, and when they withhold zakat, rain is withheld from the sky.
islam.explanation: Moral corruption and injustice are linked to drought and hardship.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s belief that injustice in a society causes the rain to fail.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; here the oppressive ruler is a punishment rather than the cause of drought. Graded hasan by some scholars.

judaism.quote_or_event: Moses warns that if Israel turns aside to serve other gods, God will shut up the heaven so that there is no rain and the land will not yield its fruit.
judaism.explanation: In the Shema, seasonable rain depends on the people’s faithfulness.
judaism.tie_back: It is the same moral link between righteousness and rain, though Deuteronomy applies it to the whole people rather than the king.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the condition is covenant loyalty, not royal justice specifically.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that when kings are unprincipled, their officials, the householders and the people follow; then the sun, moon, seasons and winds go awry, the deities are angered, the heavens do not give enough rain, and the crops ripen unevenly.
buddhism.explanation: The Adhammika Sutta traces a chain from royal injustice all the way to failed rains and failed harvests.
buddhism.tie_back: It is almost exactly the Kural’s claim that a crooked king makes the seasons fail.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.70, Adhammika Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one parallel; paraphrased from the verified SuttaCentral text.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says that on a city whose people practise violence and crooked justice, Zeus sends famine and plague together, the people waste away, women bear no children and houses dwindle. Often a whole city suffers for one wicked man.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Hesiod, crooked judgements bring natural disaster on the whole community.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Greek counterpart of the Kural’s idea that injustice from above stops the rain.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 238-247 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

philosophy.quote_or_event: “… they appeared glorious and blessed at the very time when they were full of avarice and unrighteous power. Zeus, the god of gods, who rules according to law, and is able to see into such things, perceiving that an honourable race was in a woeful plight, and wanting to inflict punishment on them …”
philosophy.explanation: Critias tells how the kings of Atlantis, once just and obedient to law, grew greedy and unjust, so that Zeus resolved to punish them; the dialogue opens by recalling that the island was later sunk by an earthquake.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato links the injustice of rulers to a cosmic punishment of their whole land, a distant parallel to the Kural's failed seasons and rain.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett). Next-best match: the dialogue breaks off before the punishment, and there is no mention of rain or seasons; the shared idea is only that unjust rule brings divine ruin on the land.

kurals.tamil:
ஆபயன் குன்றும் அறுதொழிலோர் நூல்மறப்பர்
காவலன் காவான் எனின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aapayan kundrum aruthozhilor noolmarappar
Kaavalan kaavaan enin.
kurals.meaning: If the guardian of the land fails to protect it, the cows give less milk and the learned men of the six duties forget their scriptures.
kurals.elementary: If a school has no one looking after it, the lunch kitchen stops working and the teachers stop teaching. Soon both food and learning are gone. Valluvar says that when a king doesn’t protect his land, food (milk from cows) and learning (the old books) both start to fade.
kurals.university: ஆபயன் is ‘the yield of the cow’ (ஆ, cow, and பயன், fruit), meaning milk and its products. அறுதொழிலோர் are ‘those of the six duties’, which Parimelazhagar lists as the Brahmin’s six duties: studying, teaching, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifice, giving and receiving (ஓதல், ஓதுவித்தல், வேட்டல், வேட்பித்தல், ஈதல், ஏற்றல்). He ties the couplet to 559: without milk there is no oblation (அவி), without recitation there are no mantras, so sacrifice stops, and so the rain fails. He groups 559-560 as the evils that befall the tyrant’s land. Modern commentators widen the reference: Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘the wise’ (ஞானியர்), and Kalaignar and Sivayogi Sivakumar read ‘productive work and the major occupations decline’. The older continuous text has the sandhi form நூன்மறப்பர்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The three kinds of Fire, the three Vedas, and sacrifices with Dakshina, all become lost when the king becomes heedless.” … “Elephants and steeds and kine … all lose their vigour when the king becomes unrighteous.”
hinduism.explanation: Utathya warns Mandhatri that royal neglect brings down both the Vedic order and the vigour of cattle.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches both halves of the Kural, cattle failing and the Vedas forgotten, almost word for word.
hinduism.source: Mahābhārata, Śānti Parva, Section XCI (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on both halves; verified on sacred-texts.com.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts the good shepherd with the hired hand who abandons the flock when danger comes.
christianity.tie_back: The hireling is the Kural’s ‘guardian who does not guard’, and his flock is left exposed.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified wording; strong on the failed guardian, but it lacks the Kural’s specific consequences.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that every one of you is a shepherd and responsible for his flock: the ruler is a shepherd and responsible for his people.
islam.explanation: Rule is defined as guardianship, for which the ruler will be held to account.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s காவலன் (guardian) is the Prophet’s shepherd, whose neglect harms everyone in his care.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; strong on the guardian role, silent on the specific effects.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Pray for the welfare of the government, for were it not for the fear it inspires, every man would swallow his neighbor alive.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hanina teaches that without a protecting authority, society collapses into violence.
judaism.tie_back: It is the Kural’s point: when the guardian does not guard, the order that sustains everything else falls apart.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified wording; close on the need for a protecting ruler.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Buddha’s account of the origin of society, once theft and disorder break out the people choose one of themselves, the ‘Great Elect’ (Mahāsammata), to guard the fields and punish wrongdoers in return for a share of the rice.
buddhism.explanation: Kingship begins as a contract to protect the harvest and keep order.
buddhism.tie_back: A king who does not guard has broken the very agreement that, in the Buddhist story, created kings.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; it gives the rationale rather than the Kural’s list of consequences.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus compares Penelope’s fame to that of a blameless king who upholds justice: under such a king the earth bears wheat and barley, the trees are laden with fruit, the flocks bear young without fail, and the sea gives fish.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer ties the fertility of land and flocks to the king’s justice.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the positive side of the Kural: where the guardian guards, the herds are fruitful.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close parallel, down to the flocks; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hobbes argues that without a common power to keep order, there is no place for industry or agriculture, no arts, no letters and no society, and the life of man is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short.
philosophy.explanation: For Hobbes, the sovereign’s protection is the precondition of all production and learning.
philosophy.tie_back: Both halves of the Kural are here: livelihood fails and ‘letters’ are lost when the guardian does not guard.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a striking match on the loss of both livelihood and learning.

ytamizh-ch56.title: கொடுங்கோன்மை (The Cruel Sceptre), Chapter 56, with commentary by Mu. Varadarajan, Solomon Pappaiah, M. Karunanidhi and Sivayogi Sivakumar

thirukkuralnet-adhigaram56.title: கொடுங்கோன்மை, Adhigaram 56, Thirukkural (Kurals 551-560), with commentaries by Puliyur Kesikan, Mu. Varadarasan, Solomon Pappaiah and Mu. Karunanidhi

bhagavata-purana-canto10.title: Śrīmad Bhāgavatam (Bhāgavata Purāṇa), Canto 10: Kaṁsa’s persecution of Devakī and the Yadus, and his death

manu-buhler-8.title: The Laws of Manu, trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East vol. 25, Chapter VIII
